lessons.title: घंटा (ghaṇṭā) — "hour," literally "bell"
lessons.gloss: hour — literally "bell," from the historical practice of striking a bell to mark the hour

segments.text: Here's a word that wears its history on its sleeve: Hindi's word for "hour" is the exact same word as "bell."

blocks.title: You'll want to know — घंटा — bell AND hour, one word

segments.text: घंटा (ghanṭā) = "hour" — and it means "bell, gong" just as commonly. It comes from Sanskrit घण्टा (ghaṇṭā), "bell, gong." The connection isn't a coincidence: temples, towns, and later clock towers historically marked the passing of time by striking a bell — the hour was announced by sound, not read off a face — so the word for the bell itself came to mean the unit of time it announced. Compare this to English o'clock, itself a worn-down "of the clock," or French's il est … heures: different languages, but time-telling vocabulary keeps circling back to the instrument used to mark it.

blocks.title: Grammar Lens: बजना — "to strike, to toll"

segments.text: Hindi tells the time with the verb बजना (bajnā), "to strike, to toll" — the same imagery as a bell striking the hour:
एक बज रहा है। — "It is one o'clock." (literally "one is striking") दो बज रहे हैं। — "It is two o'clock." (literally "two are striking").

Just like Spanish switches from singular es to plural son after "one," Hindi switches बज रहा है (singular) to बज रहे हैं (plural) once the count passes one — matching the number, not just tacking on "o'clock."

segments.instruction: "ek baj raha hai" — it is one o'clock, "one is striking"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "ek baj raha hai" — it is one o'clock, "one is striking"]

segments.instruction: "do baj rahe hain" — it is two o'clock, "two are striking"
segments.source: [YOU SAY: "do baj rahe hain" — it is two o'clock, "two are striking"]

segments.text: What does घंटा literally mean besides "hour"? ("Bell, gong" — from Sanskrit ghaṇṭā.) Why did "bell" come to mean "hour"? (Because clocks/towns historically struck a bell to announce the hour.) What verb does Hindi use to tell the time, and what does it literally mean? (बजना, bajnā — "to strike, to toll," as in ek baj raha hai, "one is striking.")

lessons.title: ख (kha) — one character, met inside words you already say
lessons.gloss: the single character ख — recognised inside words you already say

needs: a pen and something to write on
your eyes, for letter shapes on the page
notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. You can listen to everything else now — leave the sections called Script you'll notice: ख and Guided Practice until you have stopped, and I will say so again when we reach it.

segments.text: Before the new one: ल — what does it do?
One character this time. Just one — and you have been saying it for pages without knowing which mark on the page it was.
It is a consonant, and in this script a consonant is never bare: it comes with an a already in it. So it is not kh, it is kha.
You already say these, and every one of them has ख (kha) somewhere inside it:
शिरोरेखा shirorekhā — the head-line that Devanagari letters hang from.
ख़ुशी — happiness / pleased to meet you.

blocks.title: Writing: ख — copy what you see

segments.text: Put your pen on ख (kha) and follow its line. Copy the shape you can see — slowly, and larger than it is printed.

This book does not yet tell you where to start the character or which way to travel. That is a real thing, taught with real variation from school to school, and it is not written down here until it can be written down with a source. Copying what is in front of you needs no such source, and it is how the shape gets into your hand in the meantime.
